meaning: Making blood cells. Think of bone marrow as the body’s blood-cell factory.
A red blood cell. Its main delivery job is carrying oxygen around the body.
A white blood cell. Different types help defend the body in different ways.
A tiny cell fragment that helps form a plug at a damaged blood vessel.
A very large bone-marrow cell that releases small pieces which become platelets.
An immune cell from the B-cell, T-cell or natural-killer-cell groups.
A white blood cell that can quickly swallow microbes. It is part of the body’s early defense.
A white blood cell that can enter tissues and develop into a cleanup cell called a macrophage.
A tissue immune cell that swallows microbes and debris, like a tiny cleanup worker.
A white blood cell with storage packets called granules. Neutrophils are one example.
A blood-cell family branch that makes red cells, platelets and several kinds of white cells.
Belonging to the red-blood-cell family, especially while the cells are developing.
An earlier cell that can develop into a more mature cell, like a trainee growing into its job.
A very immature blood-forming cell. Its meaning depends on its number, type and location.
The oxygen-carrying protein inside red blood cells. It contains iron-bearing heme groups.
The iron-containing part of hemoglobin that helps bind oxygen.
The protein-chain part of hemoglobin. Several chains fit together to make the full molecule.
A hemoglobin level below the suitable reference range, reducing the blood’s oxygen-carrying capacity.
The fraction of a blood sample’s volume occupied by red cells.
A young red blood cell that has recently left the bone-marrow factory.
Red blood cells breaking apart. The cause may be inside the body or damage to a collected sample.
An iron-storage protein. It is like a cupboard that stores iron for later use.
A protein that transports iron in the blood, like an iron-delivery vehicle.
Describing red blood cells that are smaller than the expected size.
Describing red blood cells that are larger than the expected size.
Describing red cells with less hemoglobin concentration, making them look paler.
Too few platelets. Thrombo refers to clotting cells, and -penia means a shortage.
A neutrophil count below the suitable range. A severe shortage can increase infection risk.
The material inside a cell around its nucleus, containing many of the cell’s working parts.
DNA packaged with proteins inside a cell’s nucleus, like instructions bundled for storage.
A target recognized by an antibody or immune receptor. It is often a small feature on a larger object.
An immune protein that recognizes a matching target, rather like a specially shaped detector.
A chemical message used by cells to tell other cells what to do.
A team of blood proteins that help immune defenses, for example by tagging targets or damaging some microbes.
An antibody that reacts with a target belonging to the person’s own body.
An antibody against a different person’s version of a target, such as a donor red-cell antigen.
Cells or particles clumping together, often because antibodies link them.
The body’s controlled process for stopping bleeding while keeping the rest of the blood flowing.
The clotting-protein process that builds a fibrin mesh to help stabilize a blood clot.
A blood clot forming inside a blood vessel where it may obstruct blood flow.
Breaking down a fibrin clot, like carefully removing a temporary repair when it is no longer needed.
Related to the liver; hepatocytes are the liver’s main working cells.
Related to the kidneys, the organs that help control fluid balance and remove waste.
A substance that reduces or prevents clotting. Different anticoagulants work in different ways.
The liquid left after blood has clotted; it differs from plasma, which is obtained without clotting.
The liquid part of unclotted blood, containing proteins including clotting factors.
The molecule that stores genetic instructions, like an instruction book made from four kinds of letters.
A related information-carrying molecule. Cells use RNA in reading instructions and making proteins.
A stretch of genetic instructions used to make a functional product, often a protein.
One version of a gene or genetic location, like a different edition of the same instruction.
Having two matching versions at the genetic location being discussed.
Having two different versions at the genetic location being discussed.
A laboratory copying method that makes many copies of a chosen DNA segment.
An enzyme that builds a DNA or RNA chain by adding matching building blocks.
A biological helper that speeds up a chemical reaction, like a tiny specialized tool.
A roughly round bacterium. Cocci is plural; diplococci are cells seen in pairs.
In shape descriptions, a bacillus is a rod. A coccobacillus is a short, plump rod. Capitalized Bacillus can also name a genus.
A cell’s ability to move by itself. Nonmotile means it does not move under its own power.
An outer covering around some microbes. It can affect how the immune system recognizes them.
A way cells obtain energy from chemicals such as sugars without using a normal respiratory pathway. A nonfermenter may still use sugar another way.
An enzyme-related laboratory clue about a part of cellular respiration; it is not the same as every kind of oxygen use.
An enzyme that breaks hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen.
An enzyme that breaks down urea and can release ammonia, which can make the surroundings more alkaline.
A harmful substance made by an organism. Enterotoxin means a toxin that affects the intestines.
An infection that can pass from an animal source to people.
Threadlike fungal structures. A network of these threads is called a mycelium.
A type of fungal reproductive spore. Its shape can be one clue used in identifying a fungus.
In many parasite questions, a protected resting form. In other medical contexts, cyst can mean a fluid-filled sac.
The active feeding form of certain single-celled parasites.
A test that measures or detects something. It is another word for a laboratory test method.
A comparison range from a defined group of people. Being inside it does not guarantee health, and being outside it does not prove disease.
The average: add the values and divide by how many values there are.
A number describing how spread out values are around their mean. A bigger value usually means a wider spread.
Spread compared with the average, usually calculated as standard deviation divided by mean, multiplied by 100%.
How close a measured result is to the accepted reference value.
How close repeated measurements are to each other, even if they are not all close to the reference value.
A material with an assigned value used to set a test system’s measuring relationship.
Checking suitable control materials to monitor whether a test system is performing acceptably.
Reducing concentration by adding a suitable liquid, while keeping track of how much the original sample was diluted.
Moles of dissolved substance per liter of final solution. A mole is a counting unit for tiny particles.
Moles of dissolved substance per kilogram of solvent, rather than per liter of solution.
A measure of how much light a sample absorbs. It is related logarithmically to how much light gets through.
The fraction of light that passes through a sample; percent transmittance expresses it out of 100.
A tissue sample taken for examination, often to study both cells and their arrangement.
Material withdrawn by suction for examination; a marrow aspirate helps show individual developing blood cells.
A measure of a substance’s biological activity, not simply its weight in grams.
A microbe that can grow without oxygen. Some anaerobes are harmed by oxygen, while others can tolerate it.
Bacteria present in the bloodstream. It is not automatically the same thing as sepsis.
An older term often used for a serious bloodstream infection. Modern terms distinguish bloodstream infection from the body’s harmful response called sepsis.
A life-threatening harmful response to an infection that can damage the body’s own organs.
Cancer: abnormal cells growing in a harmful, uncontrolled way. Underlying malignancy means a cancer that may be causing another finding.
The large-intestine section that helps absorb water and form stool; not the whole digestive system.
Related to the intestines, where food is digested, nutrients absorbed and waste prepared to leave the body.
An organism entering and multiplying in the body; whether it causes illness depends on the organism, location and host.
The body’s response to injury or irritation. It may involve swelling, warmth or immune-cell activity and is not always caused by infection.
A group of findings that tend to occur together; a syndrome can sometimes have several different causes.
Beginning suddenly or lasting a relatively short time; it does not automatically mean severe.
Persisting or recurring over a long time; the exact time definition depends on the condition.
Present at birth. It can have inherited or non-inherited causes.
Passed through genetic information from parent to child.
The cause of a disease. An etiologic agent is the organism or factor causing it.
An organism capable of causing disease in a suitable host or situation.
Taking advantage of a chance to cause disease, such as weakened defenses or entry into an unusual body site.
Reduced immune defenses. Different conditions affect different parts of the immune system.
Related to the body’s defenses, which recognize and respond to microbes and other targets.
An early, general defense that does not need to learn a particular target beforehand.
A target-specific immune response that develops through recognition and can form memory.
Related to substances in body fluids; in immunity it usually refers especially to antibodies.
An immune response that causes unwanted harm, such as certain allergies or other immune injuries.
The constant stem of a Y-shaped antibody, which can interact with immune cells or other defense proteins.
The target-binding arm region of an antibody. Its shape helps it recognize a matching antigen.
One antibody class. It is common in blood and is the main class that crosses the placenta to help protect a baby.
An antibody class often produced early in a response; in blood it is usually arranged as a larger multi-unit molecule.
An antibody class especially important at moist body surfaces and in secretions, such as saliva and breast milk.
An antibody class involved in many immediate allergies and some responses to parasites.
A characteristic that is expressed or can be observed, such as which blood-group markers are present.
The genetic versions a person or organism carries at the location being discussed.
Human leukocyte antigens: inherited cell-surface identity markers used by the immune system to show or recognize targets.
The compartment in many cells that holds most of their DNA instructions. Mature human red cells do not have one.
Cell structures important in energy metabolism; they also have a small amount of their own DNA.
A molecule cells use to transfer usable energy, like a small rechargeable energy token.
A helper molecule that carries electrons in cell chemistry, including energy-related reactions.
The collection of chemical reactions that keep a cell or body working.
Breaking a chemical bond using water as part of the reaction. It is one way cells split larger molecules.
An enzyme or reaction that removes an amino group from a molecule, such as an amino acid.
One of the building blocks used to make proteins.
A molecule built from amino acids; different proteins act as tools, carriers, signals or structural supports.
A group including sugars and starches; cells may use them as fuel or building materials.
A group of fat-like molecules used in cell membranes, energy storage and other jobs.
A comparison of a liquid’s density with water. In urine testing it can help describe how concentrated the sample is.
A scale describing acidity or alkalinity. Lower values are more acidic; higher values are more alkaline.
Having a pH above neutral in the conditions being discussed; basic is another word for alkaline.
Having a pH below neutral in the conditions being discussed.
The fluid surrounding the brain and spinal cord.
Inflammation of the coverings around the brain and spinal cord, often due to an infection.
An infection or inflammation affecting lung tissue; different organisms can cause it.
A small immune-system checkpoint. Lymphadenitis means inflammation of lymph nodes.
An enlarged spleen, an organ that helps filter blood and supports immune defenses.
An enlarged liver. Hepato means liver and -megaly means enlargement.
Inflammation of the bladder, often caused by an infection but not always.
Inflammation of a joint. Infection is one possible cause, but there are others.
Involving more than one kind of microbe, rather than a single species.
Red cells stacked like coins, often because of the surrounding proteins; this differs from true antibody-linked clumping.
Coming from another person of the same species, such as blood from a donor.
Coming from the same person, such as their own previously collected blood.
Giving a blood component to a patient through the circulation.
A test asking whether antibodies or complement are already attached to a patient’s red cells.
An antibody reagent that helps detect certain antibodies or complement attached to red cells.
A prepared antibody product used in selected situations to help prevent immune sensitization to the red-cell D antigen.
The immune system becoming able to recognize and respond to a target after exposure.
A way to express how far a sample can be diluted while its reaction remains detectable.
A counting unit for an enormous fixed number of tiny particles. A millimole is one-thousandth of a mole.
The combining charge used in an equivalent calculation; it helps relate particle amount to electrical charge or reaction capacity.
A way to express dissolved-particle concentration per kilogram of solvent; particle number matters, not just mass.
A way to express dissolved-particle concentration per liter of solution, which differs from osmolality’s kilogram basis.
A tiny volume: one milliliter contains 1,000 microliters.
A method that uses an electric field to separate molecules according to properties such as size and charge.
Happening at one maintained temperature instead of cycling between different temperatures.
Matching and joining complementary DNA or RNA sequences, like two correctly paired pieces of a molecular zipper.
